work_order.understanding: Issue #20 is the safety slice of epic #14 and it is greenfield. I verified independently of the proposal and the critique: there is no src/policy/, no src/executor/, no src/strategy/guardian.js, no approvals/capabilities/action_records/kill_switches/trust_ledger store anywhere under src/ or in db.js's MIGRATIONS (which end at 004_knowledge_tables, src/data/db.js:173). The approvals page today (src/web/pages.js:741-800) is a static shell: it reads raw events of type 'approval.requested' (no fixture ever writes one, so it is always empty), renders the hardcoded AUTONOMY_POSTURE constant at :734-739, and its Approve/Reject buttons at :791-792 have no listener in client.js. Nothing gates a mutation because there is no module between an ActionIntent and a provider write. I also verified two things the critique surfaced and the proposal missed: the repo already ships the atomic single-winner primitive this work needs (repositories.idempotency.claim, an INSERT OR IGNORE returning true iff this call created the claim, src/data/repositories.js:148, with a release at :158 for a failed effect), and maturityFor/policyBand are already imported by src/api/routes.js:16/19 but used only inside GET /v1/metrics (:157-158) — so the band gate has an existing, correct source of truth sitting one function away. The binding decision from the brief (and the issue body) is Meta Ads first, Google Ads later, so every write targets the Meta adapter seam. The five split criteria IAC-1..IAC-5 are each carried by one acceptance entry below.
work_order.root_cause: There is no write path to gate. The repo has no module between an ActionIntent and a provider write, so the safety contract this issue is asked for — TR-2 credential isolation, TR-3 signed capabilities, TR-4 kill switches, TR-5 nonce idempotency plus reconciliation, TR-19 per-class trust, TR-24 fail-closed writes — has no code to hold it. The approvals page cannot be more than a static shell because no approval row, receipt, capability or trust row is stored anywhere, and the autonomy posture it displays is a hardcoded array read by nothing.
work_order.approach:
Build the write path as four new modules plus one composition point, on the repo's existing patterns (additive migration, tenant-bound repositories, one pure function per rule, node:test suites mirroring src/). v5's diagnosis was right and I kept it. This revision answers the one recorded rejection by taking the reviewer's option (a) — implementing the gate — and then repairs the five places where v5's own gate was not actually the single owner it claimed to be.

ONE MINTER, ONE CHOKE POINT. The recorded rejection demanded that the trust ledger gate a write end to end, and v5 answered that correctly in principle (gate at issuance, because a capability cannot exist without passing validateIntent) but then specified the approve route with its own parallel gate, so the human-approval path — the money-moving one — skipped the micro-limit, the band and the no-evidence refusal. CORRECTED: both issuance routes (POST /v1/capabilities and POST /v1/approvals/:id/approve) call kernel.validateIntent(intent, {nowIso, trust, approval, maturity}) and nothing else may mint a capability. issueCapability takes the {ok, intent} object validateIntent returns, so a route physically cannot sign an unvalidated intent, and a static import-boundary assertion pins the only two call sites. The two routes are symmetric: the same gate, differing only in whether an approval row is supplied.

THE POSTURE LADDER, and what each rung does. monotonic, so no route can launder a class into authority:
  - shadow (or a pinned class, or one with no evidence at all) -> AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED on BOTH issuance routes, even with a valid pending approval. Shadow means authority has not been granted yet; a human approval is not a way around it. This is the fail-closed reading of TR-19 and TR-24.
  - approval-required -> issues only when a non-terminal, unexpired approval row for the same tenant and action class is supplied. The approval row is the authority; the micro-limit still applies.
  - autonomous-under-micro-limits -> issues with NO approval row. POST /v1/capabilities is that route, and it is what makes IAC-4 observable end to end.

THE FAILURE FIXTURE MUST BE APPROVABLE (corrects v5's own contradiction). v5 seeded its failure-path fixture as apr_seed_launch_1 (campaign-launch) while giving campaign-launch no ledger row, so the gate refused it outright and the provider-failure path AC-5 and the QA script depend on was unreachable through the gate it had just built. CORRECTED: the seed now carries FOUR ledger rows — campaign-status autonomous (6/6/0/0), budget-change approval-required, campaign-launch approval-required, new-geography pinned shadow — and creative-refresh alone carries no row, so the fail-closed no-evidence case is still demonstrated from real data on a real roster class rather than on the write-failure fixture. Both pending fixtures are then genuinely approvable, which is what the 'either ordering consumes exactly one item' arithmetic needs.

THE BAND IS WIRED, NOT ASSUMED. v5 listed maturity as an argument validateIntent takes and no route computes it, so in production the comparison was against undefined and failed open. CORRECTED: both issuance routes compute maturity with the maturityFor/policyBand pair the repo already uses in GET /v1/metrics (src/api/routes.js:16/19, :157-158) and pass it; and validateIntent treats a missing or non-numeric maturity as MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED, because a check that cannot read its input must not pass. The band remains the autonomy gate only — a human approval is the alternative authority for a class that has not earned autonomy (TR-7 read with TR-19) — and both directions are pinned by a test.

IDEMPOTENCY IS ATOMIC AND KEYED ON THE LOGICAL ACTION. v5's executor did getByNonce then write, which is check-then-act, and the approve route minted a fresh random nonce on every call, so a second tab or a retried POST of the same approval row produced two distinct nonces and wrote twice. CORRECTED in two parts. (1) The executor's dedupe uses the primitive the repo already ships: repositories.idempotency.claim(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before the provider write, so exactly one caller reaches the provider and a loser reads back the winner's action_records row and returns its receipt with executed:false. The claim is RELEASED on a provider refusal (the repository already exposes that at :158) so a retry is a genuine retry, which is what v5 promised and could not deliver. (2) issueCapability takes an optional nonceSeed, and the approve route passes `apr:${approval_id}`, so two approves of the same row mint the SAME nonce and collapse onto the first receipt instead of writing twice. The executor's read of action_records still runs first, so a duplicate returns its receipt even while a kill switch is active.

MICRO-LIMITS SIT ABOVE EVERY SEEDED ACTION. v5 set budget-change's limit to 250_000_000 micros (₹250) — derived from, and then set below, the seed's own stated ₹300 downside (scripts/seed.js:182) — and never pinned the seeded intent's delta_micros, so the demo success path could fail MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. CORRECTED: the seed pins apr_seed_budget_1's stored intent constraints.delta_micros to 200_000_000 (₹200, inside the limit) and apr_seed_launch_1's to 0 (campaign-launch's limit is 0), and a seed-coherence test asserts every seeded approval's delta is at or under its class limit, so the demo can never be seeded into a gate it cannot pass.

RECONCILIATION IS SCOPED TO WRITES THAT CAN BE READ BACK. createDraft has no counterpart in READ_METHODS (src/integrations/meta_ads/index.js:41-46), so v5's 're-read through the read interface' step had nothing to re-read for a launch write. CORRECTED: the ACTION_METHOD contract marks each write with its read counterpart, and a write with none is documented and tested as reconciliation:'unknown' by contract rather than left to fail or to be quietly reported as reconciled.

v5's four earlier corrections are kept because they are right and I re-checked them: the executor owns the durable nonce dedupe and runs it first, while the kernel's injected port is read-only {seen} and owns REPLAYED_NONCE in isolation; the QA script runs the idempotency step before the guardian step so no step needs a live write under a freeze; the reset step is in-place (`npm run sdlc:seed -- --reset-approvals`) because the harness owns the boot (config.yml env.boot) and src/index.js holds the SQLite handle for the process lifetime, so unlinking data/app.db would leave the server on a deleted inode; and the seed carries exactly two pending fixtures with fixed ids and distinct classes.

ALSO CARRIED from v5: ACTION_CLASSES derived from DECISION_CLASSES (src/domain/decisions.js:21-26 freezes budget-change, campaign-status, creative-refresh, campaign-launch) with new-geography as the single explicit policy-only extension; the read path for a global-scope kill switch, with no '' sentinel, so repositories.js:4's every-query-binds-tenant_id contract keeps holding; pending-vs-lapsed as a read-time predicate so an aged row can never render in both the queue and the lapsed section; the five-state loading/error/partial early-returns in approvals() preserved verbatim so test/web/pages.test.js:55-63's /stale|await|Expired|provisional/i assertion still has something to match on an empty database; expiry clamped to min(ttlMs, approval.expires_at); docs/ui.md:35's typing-free explicit confirm, so approve is two-step; and src/web/client.js's false '<100 lines' header comment corrected to the real constraint.

A pending card whose class posture is shadow or no-evidence renders its approve button DISABLED with the same rule wording the kernel enforces, so the page can never invite an action the gate refuses. This is unreachable on the seed after the fixture fix above, which is exactly why it needs a test rather than a hope.

files.change: Pure domain module, no IO. ACTION_CLASSES is DERIVED from DECISION_CLASSES imported from src/domain/decisions.js and extended by exactly one explicit policy-only entry, new-geography; each class carries {microLimitMicros, requiredMaturityBand} and POLICY_ONLY_CLASSES is exported so a caller can label those rows policy-only rather than journal-representable. Limits in integer micros (TR-1): budget-change microLimitMicros 250_000_000 / requiredMaturityBand 'protective'; campaign-launch 0 / 'protective'; creative-refresh 0 / 'moderate'; campaign-status 0 / 'emergency-only' (a status flip moves no money and is the canonical emergency-band action, so the seeded demo's immature store does not by itself make the class unauthonomous); new-geography 0 / 'strategic'. validateIntent(intent, {nowIso, trust, approval, maturity}) -> {ok,intent}|{ok:false,error} is the ONLY place a capability can be minted, so it is where the trust gate lives. Order of its checks, and the order is the contract: (1) MALFORMED_INTENT — the action class is not on the roster; (2) AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED — resolve the posture from the injected `trust` value ('autonomous-under-micro-limits' | 'approval-required' | 'shadow' | 'no-evidence'): shadow and no-evidence are refused outright even with a valid approval, and approval-required is refused unless `approval` is a row for the same tenant and action class whose status is 'pending' and whose expires_at is in the future; a mismatched, terminal or expired approval is AUTONOMY_NOT_EARNED too, with details naming which of the three failed; (3) MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED — constraints.delta_micros exceeds the class limit, checked as a safe non-negative integer and never coerced from a float or a numeric string; (4) MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED — AUTONOMOUS PATH ONLY, and FAIL CLOSED: an undefined, null or non-numeric `maturity` is blocked, never treated as 'no band to check', because a check that cannot read its input must not pass. The band is the autonomy gate and a human approval is the alternative authority for a class that has not earned autonomy (TR-7 read with TR-19): an approval-required class with a valid approval is governed by the human plus the micro-limit, and its band still stops it from ever becoming autonomous. Both directions are stated in the doc comment and pinned by a test. issueCapability(validated, {secret, policyVersion, ttlMs, nowIso, expiresAtCap, nonceSeed}) — the first argument is the {ok, intent} object validateIntent returns, NOT a bare intent, so a caller cannot sign something the kernel did not clear; it throws or rejects on anything else. Signs with node:crypto createHmac and timingSafeEqual and returns {tenant, resource, action, constraints, expiry, nonce, policy_version} plus a cap_-prefixed id; expiry is min(now+ttlMs, expiresAtCap) when a cap is passed, so a capability minted from an approval can never outlive it. When nonceSeed is given the nonce is derived deterministically from it (HMAC of seed+tenant+action+resource under the signing secret, hex-truncated), so two issuances of the SAME logical action collapse onto one nonce; without a seed the nonce is random. validateCapability(capability, {secret, nowIso, killSwitches, nonces}) -> {ok,capability}|{ok:false,error} with codes MALFORMED_CAPABILITY, BAD_SIGNATURE, EXPIRED_CAPABILITY, REPLAYED_NONCE, OVER_SCOPE (details name the violated constraint), KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE, MICRO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED. Both ports are INJECTED and non-mutating: killSwitches {isActive(scope, scopeId)}, nonces {seen(nonce)} — seen, not claim; claiming a nonce is the executor's job, and this module must never reserve one. validateCapability deliberately does NOT consult trust: the capability is signed authority, and re-gating it against live ledger state at execution time would let a later ledger edit retroactively invalidate an issued capability. Imports no driver, provider, repository, sqlite or process.env; the secret arrives as an argument only.
files.why: One minter is the answer to the recorded rejection, and making issueCapability take validateIntent's return value is what turns that from a claim into a type the routes cannot get wrong. Deriving ACTION_CLASSES from DECISION_CLASSES is what stops this becoming the two-sources-of-truth failure src/domain/decisions.js:1-8 exists to prevent. One owner per nonce check is what makes AC-1 and AC-2 simultaneously satisfiable.

files.change: Pure. scoreFor(row) over a stored ledger row {evaluated, correct, needless, downside_penalties} and postureFor(actionClass, row) -> 'autonomous-under-micro-limits' | 'approval-required' | 'shadow' | 'no-evidence', with documented thresholds (autonomous requires >= 3 evaluated for that class, precision >= 0.90 and false-intervention rate <= 0.05), a pinned flag forcing shadow regardless of score, and the distinct value 'no-evidence' for a class with no row at all (TR-24, fail closed). files.why: TR-19 needs a per-class number, and one pure function over one stored ledger is what keeps the posture table and the gate on the same source. Naming the callers explicitly is the fix for the exact contradiction the rejection cited.

files.change: createExecutor({repositories, provider, kernel, auditClock}). The only module that calls a provider WRITE_METHOD. Deliberately takes NO trust parameter: the trust gate is at issuance (src/policy/kernel.js validateIntent) and this module's doc comment says so and points at it, so the two are not confused again. execute(capability, {actor}) runs its checks in THIS order, and the order is the contract: (1) DURABLE DEDUPE FIRST, in two sub-steps that together close the race v5 left open — (1a) read action_records by nonce and, if a receipt already exists, return {executed:false, receipt_id, reconciliation} immediately without validating through the kernel and without calling the provider; (1b) ATOMIC CLAIM: repositories.idempotency.claim(tenantId, nonce, 'executor') before any provider call, so of two racing deliveries exactly one proceeds; a false return means another caller won, so wait for its action_records row and return that winner's {executed:false, receipt_id, reconciliation} with no provider call. A duplicate delivery performs no mutation, so it returns its receipt even while a kill switch is active — stated in the doc comment so no one 'fixes' it into a 409. (2) kernel validateCapability, which is where KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE and the signature/expiry/scope rejections happen. (3) resolve the write method from the capability's SIGNED action through the contract module's ACTION_METHOD map (never from anything the caller passes at execute time) and call it on the injected provider. (4) re-read provider state through the read counterpart named for that write in the contract and classify drift (reported differs from applied; source 'manual'|'platform'|'third-party' as the provider reports it, 'none' when they agree); a write with NO read counterpart — createDraft — returns reconciliation:'unknown' by contract rather than inventing a value or reporting a reconciliation it cannot compute, and this is documented on the contract, not only in the executor. (5) append the action_records receipt and an audit event carrying actor and capability id, then RELEASE the claim; return {executed:true, receipt_id, requested, reported, reconciliation, drift}. A provider refusal (ok:false) releases the claim via the repository's release (src/data/repositories.js:158), returns {executed:false, error, reconciliation:'unknown'}, writes NO action_records row, and leaves the caller's approval pending, so a retry is a genuine retry rather than a silently swallowed claim. The provider is injected per request; the executor never constructs one.
files.why: Durable nonce state lives in the repository the executor already writes, not in the per-request fake (src/api/routes.js builds a new one per request, so a fake-side dedupe could not survive the two deliveries AC-2 describes). Using the repo's own claim primitive rather than get-then-act is what makes the guarantee hold under two racing requests, and the release-on-refusal is what keeps 'a retry is a genuine retry' true.

The autonomy gate's placement at issuance rather than execution is a design argument, not a spec quotation: a signed capability is authority, and re-gating it on live ledger state at execution time would let a later ledger edit retroactively invalidate a capability a human already approved. It is pinned by a test in both directions, but a reviewer who disagrees should change the executor and that test together, deliberately.

The atomic claim closes the two-racing-deliveries race for a nonce, and the approval path's deterministic nonce closes the two-tabs-approving-one-row case. work_order.confidence_rationale: The root cause is verified three times over — mine, the proposal's and the critique's, each independently confirming there is no src/policy, no src/executor, no guardian and that the approvals page is exactly the empty static shell described — and I verified two supporting facts myself (idempotency.claim exists at repositories.js:148 with its release at :158, and maturityFor/policyBand are already imported at routes.js:16/19). A plan that can be wrong in that many mutually reinforcing ways deserves humility even after the corrections, and the implementer will be following text no proposer has validated. The other drag is unchanged and irreducible here: the maturity-band reading is an interpretation of TR-7 rather than a quotation, the autonomy the demo exercises is seeded rather than earned, and the drift source is asserted against a fake that reports whatever simulateDrift is told. What would move this up: implementing test/policy/kernel.test.js and the two racing-delivery cases in test/executor/executor.test.js first and seeing the gate hold across all four postures with the atomic claim closing the race. What would move it down: a reviewer rejecting the band reading, since AC-4's autonomous case and AC-5's approval case both run through it, or the seed's approval-required row being wrong in a way that makes the demo unapprovable again.
work_order.debate_summary: The critique was right about the diagnosis and right about four things that would have shipped broken, so most of it is folded in. I want to be specific about the disagreement, because the proposal and the critique were not equally right and neither was tidy. The critique's two BLOCKING findings are real and I confirmed both against v5's own text rather than taking them on trust. First: v5 claimed validateIntent was the only place a capability could be minted, and then specified the approve route resolving the posture itself, refusing only 'not shadow', and calling issueCapability directly — so the gate had two owners and the one that escaped was the human-approval path, the money-moving one, which skipped the micro-limit, the band and the no-evidence refusal. That is the exact defect the previous rejection was about, one layer down: v4 was caught shipping a ledger enforced by nothing, and v5 was caught shipping a gate the money path walked around. The fix is structural rather than textual — a shared issuance helper both routes call, plus issueCapability taking validateIntent's return object so a route cannot sign an unvalidated intent even by accident, plus a boundary test that pins the call sites. Second: v5 seeded its failure-path fixture as campaign-launch with no ledger row, which its own gate refuses outright, so AC-5's 502 reconciliation panel and the QA step that produces it were unreachable through the gate it had just built. One seeded ledger row fixes it, and it also lets me keep the no-evidence demonstration on creative-refresh where it costs nothing. I took the three MAJOR findings too: the band gate was wired to nothing and failed open on an undefined maturity (the fix reuses maturityFor/policyBand, already imported at routes.js:16/19 — one line of reuse, not new machinery), and validateIntent now fails closed on an unreadable input; budget-change's 250,000,000 limit sat below the seed's own 300,000,000 figure at scripts/seed.js:182 with the fixture's delta never pinned, which could break the demo's own success path; and the dedupe was get-then-act while the repo already ships the single-winner primitive the plan never used. I took the MINOR finding on createDraft having no read counterpart, and folded it as a contract property with a test rather than a comment. I also took the edge case the proposal missed entirely — a pending card whose class is shadow renders a live Approve button the gate will refuse — because the page and the gate must not disagree in the same way the plan contradicted itself twice. What I REJECTED, explicitly: the critique's suggestion to give some class a requiredMaturityBand above the seeded store's band 'so the gate is demonstrably live'. campaign-status is the only class the seed calibrates autonomous, so raising its band makes the autonomous path fail MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED and IAC-4's live case unobservable. The honest move is to wire the gate correctly and say in residual_risks that the demo does not exercise it, which I have done; a demo that demonstrates itself by refusing to run is not a demonstration. I also rejected its alternative of dropping MATURITY_BAND_BLOCKED entirely — TR-7 is in this issue's coverage list, and a roster the kernel does not gate is the same display-only defect one field over. I rejected its framing of the idempotency finding as a demand to re-key on approval id: that is the right instinct for the approval path and I folded it in as a deterministic nonce seed, but as a REPLACEMENT for the nonce it would break AC-2, whose duplicate is the same capability posted twice with no approval in the request at all. The two are complementary and the work order now carries both. Two more of its edge cases I declined to turn into design changes: the in-flight freeze straddle is unreachable while the fake's writes are synchronous and belongs with the real write path, and the unicode round-trip is already covered by the escaped-copy assertion, which I extended to include the two-step confirm state rather than treating as a new gap. I did not simply accept the critique's severity ordering either: the two blocking findings are load-bearing for the recorded rejection, the band and idempotency findings are real but do not defeat a criterion on their own, and the createDraft one is a contract statement. Separately, BOTH documents missed something and I am recording it rather than leaving it to a reviewer: v5's AC-2 says 'qa_script step 7' for the idempotency step and AC-5 says 'steps 5-6' for the two approvals, but the script has nine steps and those are steps 8 and 6-7 — the same unrenumbered-pointer error v3 was corrected for, reappearing after the script grew. I have removed the numeric pointers from the acceptance criteria entirely and named each step by its content, so a future edit to the script cannot silently invalidate a criterion. The proposal's own unknowns stay unresolved and I have not dressed them up: the capability-issuance surface is unauthenticated, the drift source is fake-only, and the live Meta mutation surface is unread by design.

WRITE_METHODS is a frozen map from a capability action to a provider method name — set_campaign_status to setCampaignStatus, update_campaign_budget to updateCampaignBudget, update_campaign_creative to updateCampaignCreative, create_campaign to createCampaign — plus a WRITE_METHOD_ARITY map naming the positional arguments each call takes, so the executor can invoke a signed action without any caller-supplied function reference. resolveWriteMethod(action) returns the method or throws a typed contract error for an unknown action; the executor calls it and nothing else resolves a write. A write returns {ok:true, data} or {ok:false, error} on exactly the read shape, with the existing META_ERROR_CODES, so the executor classifies a refusal uniformly whatever produced it. This is the only file that may name both the action vocabulary of kernel.ACTION_CLASSES and a provider method.

files.change: Give the fake the four write methods the contract map names, each recording the call on `this.writes` (an array of {action, resource, args}) and returning the {ok:true, data} shape; a write under failureMode 'quota' or 'revoked' returns the SAME readError envelope the reads already build, so AC-5's failure half needs no second injection path. Reads of a written resource return the written value, so the round trip the executor reconciles against is genuine rather than a stub. WHAT I CHANGED, AND WHY — the critique was right more often than not, so this is mostly corrections, stated first.

1. THE GATE NOW BINDS THE ACTION TO THE CLASS (the critique's first blocking finding, and it is the most serious thing in either document). v9 gave every roster class a registered action and then never compared the intent's action to it: rules (a)-(f) reference only action_class, resource and constraints, and issueCapability signs whatever action the intent carries, which is precisely what the executor resolves its write method from. So a caller posting {action_class:'campaign-status', action:'create_campaign'} satisfies every stated rule — class in roster, posture autonomous, no approval, an empty constraints object inside a 50_000_000 limit, band emergency-only — and receives a signed envelope that resolves to createCampaign. create_campaign is a legitimate WRITE_METHODS entry, so the executor's 'a forged action never reaches the provider' test cannot see it: the envelope is indistinguishable from a correct one at that layer. The whole point of a per-class trust ledger is that trust earned on a reversible, small-blast-radius action buys authority for that action and nothing else, and this is the only place that is enforced. FIXED in files[0] as rule (a2), before every approval rule, refusing with details.reason 'action-mismatch'; I pinned REFUSAL over silently overwriting the envelope's action from the roster, so a mis-paired intent is a visible 403 rather than a substitution the caller never sees. Kernel case and AC-4 both name campaign-status carrying create_campaign.

2. AC-4 NO LONGER CLAIMS MORE THAN THE ISSUE ASKS. Its check read 'while new-geography cannot execute on any route', which rules (e), assumption 3, the queue QA step and AC-7's 'no approve button is disabled for it' all forbid — the issue's own split criterion says new-geography stays in 'shadow or approval', and shadow in this design means never-autonomous, not never-possible. Left alone, an implementer reading the criterion would harden rule (e) to refuse new-geography even with an approval and break three other places; or QA would fail the ticket against a sentence the design never promised. The check is rewritten to the rule the server enforces, and the QA step now says the same thing.

THE RESET CLEARS THE RECEIPT STORE (the critique's third finding, and it is the one that would have failed the ticket on its second run). v9's reset returned approvals to pending and cleared their receipt_id, and named action_records NOWHERE. The decide route checks action_records for the nonce 'apr_'+approvalId BEFORE the approval's status, by design, so a surviving receipt from a previous run makes the next approve return 200 {executed:false, receipt_id: <stale>} with no execution and no status write: the card never leaves the queue, the heading count never drops, and a success toast naming last run's receipt is still shown. Every browser criterion hangs off this one command and QA is deliberately given no memory of its previous runs. FIXED in files[12] — the reset deletes the seeded tenant's apr_seed_* action_records rows and the matching idempotency_keys rows — with a test that resets twice, approves, and asserts executed:true with a fresh receipt.

risks: Highest-risk slice in the project: money movement, auth-equivalent capabilities, credential isolation and kill switches. test/executor/credential-isolation.test.js is the static import-boundary check TR-2 asks for and is a required part of this work order — and its assertion is on the signing literal's LOCATION and COUNT, so it can actually fail.

The autonomy gate makes an executive call about what may execute without a human. If validateIntent admits something it should not, a write happens with no approval. It therefore fails closed on every ambiguous input — an unknown class, a missing or unrecognised posture, a malformed approval row, a missing, null or non-finite maturity, and a tenant with no raw events at all are all refusals, not defaults. The maturity cases are not hypothetical: policyBand(NaN) returns 'strategic', and the metric route's own ternary substitutes 0 for no data at all, so the absence of evidence is the direction this gate must never fail in.

POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface: the trust ledger gates ISSUANCE and never execution, by design, because a signed capability is the attestation and a second owner for one check would let a trust-row edit retroactively invalidate a correctly issued capability. Its only controls are signature, expiry, scope, tenant and the kill switch. With the signing secret defaulting to a public dev constant, that surface is forgeable by anyone holding the source. This is bounded today only by the fact that the only writable provider is the in-memory fake; it is the first thing to revisit when a live write path lands.

This slice adds no real mutation path: live.js gains no write method and the process holds no ad credentials. That is deliberate, and it means an approved budget change is NOT visible on a later dashboard load — the receipt's reconciliation record is the evidence, not the campaign table. QA should not expect / to change after an approval.

The capability signing secret defaults to a dev-only value in every environment that exists, because project.md records no deployment. The mitigation is that the default is named, warned about once at startup, overridable via POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET, and confined to one file by an executable test — not that it is removed, which would leave CI and browser QA unable to verify a signature deterministically.

Migration 006 must stay additive and idempotent: every statement is CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS and the five existing migrations are untouched, because a runner may already hold a database from earlier slices. The number is 006 and not 005 because 005_opportunity_experiment_tables is already in the array at src/data/db.js:223.

Two schema-level constraints are load-bearing and read as ordinary: UNIQUE(tenant_id, nonce) rather than a global nonce, and a NOT NULL scope_id. Both exist because of SQLite behaviours no reviewer reads off the schema at a glance — NULLs are distinct in a rowid PRIMARY KEY, so an ON CONFLICT target with a NULL scope_id never matches and a re-enable can never clear the freeze. The guardian test that triggers the same kind twice is what holds that honest.

The isActive union query is the one line in this change that can silently break tenant isolation while looking correct: its second disjunct must bind tenant_id, because it is the only clause that can match a global row. The reverse-direction case in test/data/tenant-isolation.test.js is what holds it.

Approvals rows are mutable by design while action_records and guardian_incidents are append-only with storage triggers; a re-enable therefore records on kill_switches and audit_events and never updates an incident. resetSeededKillSwitches is a deliberate, documented fixture exception reachable only from the seed.

The micro-limits and requiredMaturityBands in ACTION_CLASSES are declared policy constants chosen by this plan, not derived from anything in the repo. They are pinned here and in the seed, and every seeded approval is asserted admissible against them, so changing any of them is a one-line edit the tests will notice — but a human may reasonably want different numbers. No class requires a band above 'emergency-only', which is what makes the demo work and also what means the live demo never exercises the band floor in its restrictive direction.

src/web/client.js grows well past the '<100 lines' its own header comment already exceeded at 154. There is no build step to split it, so the cost is accepted and the false comment is corrected rather than left standing.

Rule (a2) exists because the gate was, until this revision, calibrating a CLASS while signing an ACTION. The same family of hole is worth watching in every later slice that adds a class to the roster: a class is only as safe as the binding between the thing trust was earned on and the thing that gets signed.

The reset is now a load-bearing part of the demo rather than a convenience. A QA run that does not begin with it, or a seed reset that stops covering the receipt store, fails at the approve step with a stale receipt id and no other symptom — which is exactly the shape that sends the next person looking in the wrong module.

The posture table is rendered on a null scope now, with every class reading 'approval required' and no evidence. That is the fail-closed answer and it keeps the existing page suite honest, but it means a first-run database shows a table of five refusals, which is a real screen and not a neutral one.

alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It produces the same five rendered rows as the resolution I chose, but it makes two high-risk classes' postures depend on precision thresholds computed from two and one observations. A pinned row is the honest statement for a class that should never be autonomous regardless of what three observations say, and it leaves exactly one score-near-the-line case (budget-change), which is where the calibration is actually being demonstrated.

alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It breaks the three-label invariant AC-7 asserts, and it conflates two different things: a class with no evidence about it and a class that has evidence saying 'approval required' both fail closed, but only one of them has ever been measured. alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The issue's out_of_scope defers only 'Autonomous strategic actions BEYOND micro-limits', so micro-limit autonomy is in scope, and IAC-4's verb is 'executes'. alternatives_considered.approach: Move the posture check into the executor as well as at issuance, so /v1/actions/execute is also gated on the ledger
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Two owners for one check, and the second is wrong: a trust row edited between issuance and execution would retroactively invalidate a correctly signed capability, so a legitimate write would fail for a reason the signer cannot see. validateIntent is the single gate and a signed capability is the attestation; the executor re-checks only what can change underneath a capability — signature, expiry, scope, tenant, kill switch. The asymmetry is accepted and stated in files[3], files[4] and risks rather than papered over, because the honest version of this design is that the execute surface is a bearer-token surface.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give the kernel a mutating {claim(nonce)} port and let it reject a replay before the executor's action_records lookup
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This contradicts AC-2: the second delivery would get an error envelope instead of the original receipt, and the kernel has no way to produce a receipt_id. The executor dedupes and claims first, the kernel's port stays read-only {seen}, REPLAYED_NONCE is documented as the defence-in-depth branch the executor shadows, and both criteria hold.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the executor's dedupe as a bare read of action_records by nonce, with no atomic claim
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is what an earlier proposal specified and it does not close what the plan says it closes. Two deliveries that interleave — two tabs, a retried POST against a slow provider — both pass the read and both reach the provider, so the second-browser-tab race stays open on the one surface that moves money. The repo already ships claim/record/release on repositories.idempotency (src/data/repositories.js:148-160) and src/workflows/scheduler.js:71-79 uses exactly that shape, so the fix is a reuse rather than a new mechanism.

alternatives_considered.approach: Move the dev-default signing literal into a new src/policy/secret.js and have both index.js and routes.js import it
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It resolves a contradiction but makes src/api/routes.js import a signing constant from src/policy/, which is the very clause the isolation test uses to say routes.js does not hold key material — it trades one required test that cannot pass for a weaker one that can. Keeping the literal in routes.js, which is the composition point that must have a fallback for the call sites that pass no policyConfig, keeps index.js the only reader of the env variable and keeps the isolation test's meaning intact.

alternatives_considered.approach: Let the maturity helper keep the metric route's 0-hours substitution for a tenant with no events, and rely on the kernel's finite-number guard alone
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A no-data tenant is handed a legitimate 0 before the kernel ever sees an absent value, and 0 is the emergency-only band, which every seeded class requires — so a brand-new tenant would execute autonomously with a healthy-looking band. That contradicts the fail-closed claim in risks[1], and the fix is one line in a helper this change is already writing.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep a freshly minted nonce per issuance and instead make the client disable the approve button until a response arrives
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The guard is per-tab and client-side, so a second tab or a lost response still writes twice, and the failing case is precisely the one where the operator most needs to retry. Deriving the nonce from the approval and looking the receipt up before the status check makes the server idempotent, which is the only place this is actually true.

alternatives_considered.approach: Let validateIntent read the approvals and raw-events repositories directly instead of taking the approval row and maturity as arguments
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would make the policy kernel impure and break the import-boundary test — the kernel exists to be a deterministic pure function. It would also make the maturity SOURCE implicit, which is the defect this work order fixes: the source is named in one place, the route, and pinned by a test.

alternatives_considered.approach: A single combined src/policy/safety.js holding kernel, trust, guardian and executor
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It would put the provider write call in the same file as the policy rules and the HMAC secret's reach, which is precisely the boundary TR-2 requires be provable with a static import check.

alternatives_considered.approach: JWT library (jose) for capability signing
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A new runtime dependency for what node:crypto's createHmac with timingSafeEqual does in a few lines; conventions require stdlib first with a one-line justification and there is none to give.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep one pending approval fixture and rewrite the script to approve the same still-pending item twice
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes a browser criterion depend on a subtle two-step order on one item, and a QA run that succeeds on the first click leaves nothing to fail on the second. Two distinct fixtures satisfy both orderings and give the posture table its executed and lapsed sections for free.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep a '' sentinel tenant_id for the global kill switch and give isActive a special two-scope read
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It needs a deliberate exception to the module contract at src/data/repositories.js:1-7, and a reader who misses the exception silently loses the global freeze. A global-scope row carrying a real tenant_id, read by the same union query with both disjuncts tenant-bound, needs no exception at all.

alternatives_considered.approach: Let issueCapability overwrite the envelope's action from ACTION_CLASSES instead of refusing a mis-paired intent
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It closes the hole silently: a caller who asks to spend campaign-status autonomy on a campaign creation gets a signed capability for a status change and no error, and the mismatch is invisible everywhere downstream. Refusal makes it a 403 with a named reason, costs one rule, and is testable from outside the module. A later slice may still normalise the action at the route boundary — but it should do so as a visible rewrite, not as a quiet default inside the signer.

alternatives_considered.approach: Make AC-7 and qa_script order-insensitive instead of pinning the roster order (the critique's second option)
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Row order on a five-row posture table is the operator's reading order and the recorded review already rejected this slice once for a plan and a criterion that described different tables. Set-insensitivity removes the one property that would have caught a drifted order, and it would still leave files[0] and the test asserting different sequences. Pinning the literal keeps the derivation's drift protection through a separate set-equality assertion, which is where it belongs.

alternatives_considered.approach: Have the decide route check the approval's status before the receipt lookup, so a reset that leaves receipts behind cannot short-circuit a fresh decision
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It trades a QA-fixture bug for a real one. Receipt-before-status is what makes a redelivered approve idempotent instead of a 409 (AC-2, and the plan's own second-delivery test), and a second tab or a retried POST is exactly the case where a 409 tells the operator their action failed when it succeeded. The correct place to fix a stale receipt is the reset that created it.

alternatives_considered.approach: Drop the trust_ledger PRIMARY KEY and resolve a class's posture by 'the most recent row wins'
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Not seriously considered: the key is already pinned in the migration and the plan's own reason for it — one displayed posture and one enforced posture read from one row — is the property this design exists to provide. Recorded here because the critique raised it, so the dismissal is on the record rather than silent.

assumptions: The QA harness owns the server boot (.sdlc/config.yml:107 env.boot = npm run sdlc:serve) and can run `npm run sdlc:seed -- --reset-approvals` against the same ./data/app.db the running server has open. The script entry is `node scripts/seed.js` (package.json:13), so npm passes the flag through as argv; if the harness cannot pass extra argv the same reset is reachable as `node scripts/seed.js --reset-approvals`. Either way it must not unlink the database file or restart the server. This is the assumption every browser criterion depends on and it is the one thing I could not verify from the code. What the code DOES settle: the database is opened with no busy timeout (src/data/db.js:278-296), so this slice adds PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000 and qa_script step 2 states the expected busy-error text so a lock is distinguishable from an empty queue.

Maturity for the gate is the tenant's data-through age computed over FUNNEL_TYPES-filtered raw events through the repo's own dataThrough/maturityFor/policyBand, in one helper extracted from GET /v1/metrics. On seed data the JOURNEY events are stamped by occurredAt() at scripts/seed.js:381, six hours before the run, so the age is about 6h and maturityFor(6) is about 0.0625 — an earlier proposal cited :72,84,96 (decision and learning fixtures, not raw events) and read the age as 0; neither is right and both land in the same band. 0.0625 is 'emergency-only', so the seeded classes carrying requiredMaturityBand 'emergency-only' are admitted, and because the floor rises with maturity a database seeded weeks ago reads 'strategic' and is still admitted. A tenant with NO events is not admitted at all — the helper returns null and the kernel refuses it as 'maturity-unknown'.

The approve path supplies the approval row it is executing to validateIntent, so a non-autonomous class is admitted by an explicit human approval and refused without one, and an autonomous class is admitted whether or not a row is supplied. I read IAC-4's 'new-geography stays in shadow or approval' as sanctioning exactly this: shadow means never autonomous, approval means a human may still say yes. This is also why the page renders no disabled approve button — a control that says 'you may not approve this' would contradict the rule the server enforces.

The seed's trust-ledger numbers (6/6/0 autonomous, 3/2/1 approval-required, two pinned shadows, one class with no row) are calibration fixtures chosen by this plan, and they are what make the enforced posture and the displayed posture agree. If a human wants different numbers the gate changes with them; what must not happen is the two surfaces being derived from different data, which is why both read trust.postureFor over the same rows and why a test asserts the rendered table against the gate's own verdict.

An approval is created by strategy code in a later slice; this slice only decides, executes and records, so the seed and the tests are the only approval writers. This is also why nothing in this change can detect two pending approvals for the same resource — no component here proposes, so the duplicate case is deferred rather than solved.

A signed capability is valid on its own authority for its whole lifetime and is not re-checked against the trust ledger at execute time (see alternatives_considered for why a second owner is worse). One consequence I am choosing rather than discovering: a capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch. That is recorded in residual_risks rather than left to be found.

The QA harness can pass extra argv to the seed script, so `npm run sdlc:seed -- --reset-approvals` reaches `node scripts/seed.js --reset-approvals`. This is now a stronger dependency than it was in v9, because the reset also clears the receipt store: if the flag does not arrive, no browser step is reachable rather than only the approve step.

The seeded class list and its order are policy constants this plan pins, not values derived from the repo. new-geography is a fourth seeded row precisely because the recorded review rejected a criterion that asked the table to show a posture no ledger row could produce; if a human wants different calibration numbers, the seed and the gate change together or the seed-coherence test in test/api/actions.test.js fails.
unknowns: The exact Graph mutation endpoints and field names a live write would use. Deliberately untouched: live.js gains no write method, so no write contract beyond the typed shapes is committed to here.

How a real provider reports drift source. The fake reports it from simulateDrift and the executor classifies whatever the provider names; against a live provider this needs a platform-side signal this slice does not have.

Whether the QA harness runs each qa_script step against the same server process. Every step is written to be safe either way — the reset is in-place and no step boots or kills the server — but if steps are split across processes, the last step's freeze outlives the process and the next run's reset still clears it.

Whether a human will want a third posture between 'shadow' and 'approval-required'. TR-19 and IAC-4 only name the two, so this work order implements the two and the table's three-label invariant would need widening if a third appears.

Whether the approval-derived nonce scheme survives a later slice where a single approved intent legitimately needs more than one provider write (for example updateBudget then setCampaignStatus). The scheme is correct for one-write-per-approval, which is all this slice has; a multi-step action would need a sub-nonce and that is a design question for the slice that first needs it.

Whether any band edge will move as account-specific bands replace the default lag model (TR-7's 'bands become account-specific over time'). BAND_ORDER is exported and pinned against policyBand's current output in a test, so a re-ordering would fail loudly rather than quietly invert the floor — but the right band per class is a calibration question this slice cannot settle from the code.
residual_risks: QA reads these first. (1) POST /v1/actions/execute is a bearer-token surface whose only control is the signing secret, and the secret has a public dev default — a capability forged offline is accepted without the trust ledger ever being consulted, and a cross-tenant envelope is refused only because this work order adds the TENANT_MISMATCH check. (2) The two-step confirm, the retry safety and the meta_error propagation are enforced SERVER-side because the repo has no DOM harness; the REST of client.js — the in-flight guard, the toast fill, the pending-count decrement, the reason input surviving a failure — has NO executable coverage and is verified by qa_script steps 7-8 only. Read those assertions as human observation, not as a regression net. (3) The signing secret's dev default is live wherever POLICY_SIGNING_SECRET is unset, which today is everywhere; the blast radius is bounded only by the fact that the only writable provider is the in-memory fake. (4) .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md and environment.md are NOT updated by this work order — the triage finding is correct that a ticket branch may not touch them, and qa_script is a substitute, not a replacement. They stay stale about the new data-testids (guardian-banner, posture-table, posture-row-<action_class>, approval-toast, approval-reconciliation), the new /v1 routes and the --reset-approvals re-run contract until the Librarian's branch is refreshed. (5) A capability issued before a freeze and executed after the re-enable is admitted, because validateCapability sees an inactive switch; nothing records that the capability predates the freeze. (6) Two pending approvals for the same action_class and resource both execute — correct for this slice, since nothing here proposes, and asserted so a future dedupe is deliberate. (7) No seeded class requires a band above 'emergency-only', so the live demo never exercises the maturity floor in its restrictive direction: it is covered by test/policy/kernel.test.js with explicit maturity fixtures, and a change to the band thresholds or to a class's requiredMaturityBand would NOT redden the live demo — only the kernel suite notices. The same is true of the micro-limits. (8) The ?meta_error simulation is a URL-level switch with no on-page indication: a bookmarked /approvals?meta_error=quota makes every approval fail silently with no way to clear it from the page. Pre-existing on /, unchanged here, filed in out_of_scope. (9) With buildApp's policyConfig optional, the dev-default secret applies inside every existing test, so signature tests pass against a secret no test controls. (10) AC-2's 'executes exactly once' is verified two different ways on purpose and QA should not expect one to substitute for the other: the single provider write is a test assertion over one injected instance, and the live step can only show a stable receipt id, because the route builds a provider per request. (11) The five-state shells, the 404 envelope for unknown /v1 paths and the fake provider's cross-request statelessness are contracts this change edits or extends; test/web/approvals.test.js, test/api/*.test.js and test/integrations/meta_ads.test.js cover them explicitly, so read those assertions as the regression net rather than trusting this description. (12) The posture table is a five-row fixture, not a live surface: it reads the trust_ledger at render time so it is current, but nothing in this slice WRITES a trust_ledger row in production, because the writer is strategy code in a later slice. If a human edits a row directly in the database the table moves and the gate moves with it, which is the intent.

(12) The posture table's first column now reads roster slugs ('campaign-status') where it read prose ('Campaign status change'). Nothing asserts those strings, so no test will catch a future revert or a copy regression; the change is recorded here for the Librarian to reconcile against docs/ui.md along with the selectors and environment files this work order cannot touch.

(13) The reset's receipt deletion is enforced by a test in test/api/approvals.test.js, not by a schema rule. A later slice that seeds a differently-named approval and forgets the apr_seed_ prefix pattern reintroduces exactly the second-run failure this revision fixed, and nothing else in the suite would notice.

(14) The new null-scope posture table (five rows, all 'approval required', no evidence) is what a tenantless database renders. It is the fail-closed answer and it keeps the existing page suite green, but it is a screen nobody has looked at, because the seeded demo never has a null scope.
validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: The root cause is verified and not in doubt: there is no src/policy/, no src/executor/, no guardian, the six safety tables are absent, and the approvals page is the static shell both prior documents describe, so the design rests on code I read rather than on a citation I believed. I re-checked the critique's evidence myself on the ones that were load-bearing and they hold: DECISION_CLASSES really is frozen with budget-change first, firstTenant really does return null and the page suite really does render all five routes that way, resolveState really does return 'ideal' for any existing tenant, idempotency.claim really is an INSERT OR IGNORE used the same way by the scheduler, and the trust_ledger key the critique says is missing is in fact pinned in migration 006. I am below the proposal's 78 on purpose, for a reason that is about the artifact and not about the design: this is the fourth round, the previous one was rejected for exactly this family of defect, and both the critique and this revision found further instances of it after the previous round claimed to have swept the file. Rule (a2) is the worst of them — a per-class trust ledger that calibrates a class but signs an action is not a gate, it is a comment — and it survived three reviews of a plan that was otherwise extremely careful. Every correction is now named in files[], tests[] or acceptance[] with the mechanism spelled out rather than asserted, and the two that would have failed the ticket outright (the action binding, the reset's receipt store) have tests that are red until they are right. What would move this up: an implementer writing test/policy/kernel.test.js and test/api/actions.test.js FIRST and finding that the band floor, the finite-and-null maturity refusals, the autonomous-plus-approval case, the action binding, the atomic claim and the receipt-before-status ordering all hold together — that intersection is where the autonomy path, the approval path and idempotency meet, and it is where a wrong reading shows up fastest. What would move it down, and it is not far: QA discovering it cannot pass --reset-approvals against the live server's open handle. That single command is now the precondition for every browser criterion, I cannot verify it from the code, and if it fails this number is too high. If QA hits a busy lock even with the 5s timeout, stop and route to a human rather than working around it.
validated_work_order.debate_summary:
The critique was right more often than not and I am not going to dress that up. I re-checked every finding against the file and line it cited: eight of eleven held, including both it marked blocking and five of its six majors. The first blocking finding is the most serious defect either document contained, and it is worth being precise about why: the plan gave every action class a registered provider action, wrote the executor to resolve its write method from the SIGNED action, and then never once compared the two — so the ledger's entire claim, that trust earned on a reversible status flip buys authority for that and nothing else, was enforced nowhere. Fixing it is one rule and one test case. The second blocking finding is the same shape one layer up: AC-4 asserted a stronger rule than the design enforces and than the issue asks for, and I rewrote the criterion rather than hardening the kernel, because the issue's split criterion says new-geography stays in 'shadow or approval' and shadow here means never-autonomous, not never-possible. Both of the reset and the roster order are the same failure mode a third time: a thing that a QA reader compares literally — a receipt id, a row position — was left resting on a derivation or an omission that produces a different literal. I folded every one of these into files[], tests[] or acceptance[] rather than arguing any of them away.

WHAT I DISMISSED, EXPLICITLY. The critique's finding that the trust_ledger's key is never specified is FALSE, and I want it on the record rather than dropped: files[5] pins PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, action_class) in migration 006, which is the correct key, and repositories.trustLedger.upsert is already specified against it. The finding is right that a duplicate row would let the displayed and enforced postures disagree, and that observation is a good one, but it is not a gap in this plan — I strengthened the migration entry to say why the key is load-bearing rather than moving anything. Two of its regression risks are real and I took them (the append-only surface list, the write-interface check against the fake only); its other regression risks are the same ones the design already handles and I noted them rather than rewriting files. Its finding about AC-5 is right about the AC and wrong that nothing covers the empty state — qa_script and two test cases reach it — so I fixed the criterion's order and its rationale and said so rather than accepting the larger claim.

WHERE WE STILL DISAGREE. Its severity framing on the ledger-gates-issuance-not-execution asymmetry is not in this round at all, and I keep the design's position: one owner for the gate, a signed capability as the attestation, and the execute surface honestly described as a bearer-token surface whose only control is a signing secret with a public dev default. That is a real alarm about a real property of this slice, and it is the price of a recorded choice rather than something a critic can settle. I am also not adopting its suggestion that the execute path be re-gated against the ledger; a trust row edited between issuance and execution must not retroactively invalidate a correctly signed capability, and the plan says so where the next reader will find it.

WHAT BOTH DOCUMENTS MISSED, which I take as the honest summary of this round: an absent delta_micros on the one class that requires one, a fake-provider write against a resource its fixtures do not contain, and the deliberate header/banner contradiction under ?state=empty. None is large; all three are the same kind of thing — a behaviour the plan did not state, in a slice where an unstated behaviour is read by an implementer under time pressure. Four rounds in, the pattern is consistent: this artifact keeps producing unstated decisions in the one slice where a wrong reading moves money, and every round's corrections have come from re-reading the same files rather than from any new insight about the problem. That is worth saying plainly, because it is the strongest argument for the review stage this route carries and for a human reading the diff against files[0] rather than against this summary.
